what_its_for: Bevacizumab-maly is a cancer medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum), lung cancer, kidney cancer, cervical cancer, ovarian cancer, and certain brain tumors. It works by blocking the growth of new blood vessels that tumors need to grow and spread.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes between 30 minutes and 90 minutes, depending on how well you tolerate it. You will be watched closely during and after your infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight, the type of cancer you have, and the other medicines you are taking. Doses are usually given every 2 or 3 weeks. It is very important to keep all of your scheduled infusion appointments. Do not skip any doses without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your care team will help you get back on schedule safely.
storage: You will not need to store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by the pharmacy or hospital. If you are told to keep any supplies at home, store them in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it away from light and out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor before starting this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Avoid any dental procedures or surgeries during treatment unless absolutely necessary, and always tell your surgeon or dentist you are receiving this medicine. Avoid activities that increase your risk of injury or bleeding, such as contact sports. Do not take aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, or other blood-thinning medicines without first checking with your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: severe headache, sudden vision changes or loss of vision, chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, unusual bleeding from any part of your body, severe stomach pain or vomiting, signs of infection (fever over 100.4°F, chills, burning when urinating), wounds that will not heal, sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, difficulty speaking, seizures, swelling or pain in your legs, or any serious allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: This medicine works continuously while you are receiving it, but you may not feel or notice its effects right away. Your doctor will check how well it is working through regular scans and blood tests. It may take several weeks to months before the benefits are fully visible on scans. Continue all scheduled appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. It can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Older adults (65 and over): Older patients may have a higher risk of serious side effects such as blood clots, stroke, heart attack, and severe bleeding. Your doctor will monitor you very closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions before starting treatment. Children: The safety and effectiveness of this medicine in children have not been fully established. Always share your full medical history with your care team.
